Invalidate

/in-VAL-ih-dayt/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Invalidate means to make something no longer legally or officially valid or binding, often because of a flaw or technicality rather than a deliberate act.

A single missing signature on the final page was enough to invalidate the entire insurance claim.

Worked Example

Priya spent months negotiating the sale of her family's bakery. On signing day, her lawyer noticed that the notary had stamped the wrong page of the contract. That single clerical error was enough to invalidate the whole agreement, and the sale could not close until a corrected contract was drawn up. Nobody had acted in bad faith; a technical flaw alone had made the document legally worthless.

The contract became legally void because of a technical flaw, not as a punishment, which is exactly the situation invalidate describes.

How Invalidate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

void

void: to cancel something so it has no legal force

nullify

nullify: to make something count for nothing

Antonyms

uphold

uphold: to confirm that something stands and remains in force

ratify

ratify: to formally approve something and make it official

How Strong Is It? — undermine → invalidate → annul

undermine vs. invalidate

undermine vs. invalidate: Undermine is weaker than invalidate: undermining a contract merely weakens confidence in it, while invalidating it makes it legally void.

annul vs. invalidate

annul vs. invalidate: Annul is stronger than invalidate: an annulled agreement is wiped away as if it had never existed at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: not

Root — valid

Root — valid: from Latin validus, strong or effective

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: to make or cause to become

Put it together

Put it together: Invalidate is built from Latin in-, meaning not, plus validus, meaning strong or effective. Literally, to invalidate something is to make it not strong, so it can no longer stand on its own legally.

Use the root in a new word: validate

Use the root in a new word: validate: The clerk stamped the parking ticket to validate it, confirming it was officially good for a free exit.

Word Choice

formal, legal and technical register

Invalidate usually happens because of a flaw, error, or technicality; nobody has to intend it as a punishment. Compare rescind, which is a deliberate, formal cancellation of a law, order, or agreement by a governing body, while invalidate describes something becoming legally void, often on its own.
